transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Mia Torres (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (Arcadian Head of ML), Jonas Miller (CTO), Sara Gupta (Infra Lead)

Summary (auto-gen - may be rough):
Arcadian is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private Redwood deployments focused on cost per inference and unit economics. Primary concerns: per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, latency SLOs for trading signals, budget caps and predictable monthly commit for dedicated. Next steps include pricing spreadsheet, workload sample, and technical deep dive.

Transcript:
[00:00] Mia: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time, um, appreciate it. quick intros, I'm Mia, AE at Redwood.
[00:06] Evelyn: Hi Mia, Evelyn Park, head of ML at Arcadian. Jonas and Sara are with me.
[00:10] Jonas: Hey all.
[00:12] Sara: Hi.
[00:14] Liam: Liam Chen, solutions engineer. we'll focus on the cost and perf side.
[00:18] Mia: Great. Quick agenda - understand your workloads, budget targets, and then go through per-token pricing and levers like batching, KV cache, quantization, and finally next steps. Sound good?
[00:27] Evelyn: Yep. We're running a couple of real-time models for signal extraction and a batch scoring job overnight. Latency for realtime is critical, sub-100ms if possible, for some paths. Batch can be lenient.
[00:38] Jonas: Also we care about cost predictability. We're currently paying per-request on another vendor and it's spiking. We want to understand where hosted makes sense vs committing to dedicated capacity or even private for compliance.
[00:48] Mia: Totally. Can you share rough QPS and sequence lengths? even ballpark helps.
[00:52] Evelyn: For realtime, it's 200-400 requests per second at peak; typical prompt length 200-400 tokens, response 50-150 tokens. For batch, it's 500k to 2M records nightly, long contexts up to 2k tokens but throughput tolerant.
[01:10] Liam: Okay so two patterns - latency-sensitive small responses and high-throughput batch with long sequences. That shapes batching and kernel choices.
[01:18] Jonas: On budget - we have a monthly cap target around $40k for inference. We're evaluating if hosted per-token can hit that or if dedicated reserved makes more sense.
[01:27] Mia: Understood. Our hosted model pricing is per-token and we have tiered discounts at higher volumes; dedicated is a reserved GPU pool with predictable hourly cost which converts to a per-token equivalent depending on utilization. We also recommend caching + batching to reduce effective token counts.
[01:41] Evelyn: Walk us through a concrete example: if we do hosted with your standard model, what would per-token look like and how do batching/caching change it?
[01:50] Liam: Sure. High-level: hosted per-token for our standard open-models sits in the range X cents per 1k tokens at our public list, but for a customer at your volume we'd typically model effective cost with caching and batching. Example scenario - without caching, per-inference cost = per-token * (prompt tokens + response tokens). With KV/prefix cache for repeated prefixes like system instructions or market context, you can avoid re-tokenizing/re-computing prefix every time - so for your realtime pipeline with stable prompt prefix you might save 60-80% on prompt tokens. Then batching for batch jobs aggregates many requests to amortize kernel overhead, which can drop cost per token significantly for throughput workloads.
[02:28] Sara: Sorry, Liam, that X cents number - can you be more specific? our finance team needs numbers.
[02:32] Liam: Right. Public list numbers are, uh, say $0.03 per 1k input tokens and $0.06 per 1k output tokens for a mid-size 70B class open model—this is illustrative, we'll send the exact spreadsheet. But the key is effective cost after caching. For example, a 250-token prompt where 200 tokens are cached prefix reduces billed prompt tokens to 50 per request, so you only pay for 50+response tokens. So if you have 100 QPS with that pattern, the difference is substantial.
[03:01] Evelyn: That helps. For our peak 400 rps, with 80% prefix reuse, that saves big. But what about latency impact? we need sub-100ms.
[03:12] Liam: Caching is low-latency, it's in-memory KV cache on the serving nodes. For prefixes stored in KV cache, the runtime uses cached KV cache vectors to skip recompute, so latency improves. There's also batching tradeoffs - small batch sizes preserve latency, larger batch sizes push throughput. On dedicated you can tune autoscale and reserved pools to target latency SLOs with headroom.
[03:33] Jonas: So hosted vs dedicated: hosted is easiest but variable cost; dedicated gives predictability but you pay for reserved GPU even when idle. How do you model break-even?
[03:43] Mia: We usually run a utilization-based break-even model. Take your expected peak and baseline utilization, estimate tokens per month, and compare hosted per-token spend vs dedicated monthly commit divided by expected served tokens. For example, if your utilization is >60-70% on a reserved pool, dedicated often becomes cheaper. But we also factor in burst capacity and reliability needs. We'll send a two-sheet model that shows per-token equivalence at different utilization levels.
[04:04] Sara: How does quantization fit in? can you get the same quality with 4-bit quantized models and how much cost reduction?
[04:10] Liam: Good question. Quantization reduces GPU memory and can fit more replicas per GPU; that lowers effective per-token compute cost. For many workloads, 4-bit (or int8/quant) variants deliver near-identical quality; we have model-specific recommendations. Cost reduction varies but typical is 20-40% on compute cost depending on model and sequence lengths. We'll call out which model variants are verified.
[04:36] Evelyn: We also have compliance: some signals include customer PII. For that we might need private deployment or VPC. How does private affect unit economics?
[04:46] Mia: Private/VPC adds a platform licensing and infra cost. If you self-host on-prem, you'll have fixed infra costs (hardware amortization, ops). Per-token then depends mostly on utilization and your infra efficiency. For many regulated teams, the incremental per-token may be higher than hosted but you gain compliance control. We can model private vs dedicated committed costs too.
[05:06] Jonas: What about autoscaling on dedicated? If we reserve X GPUs but have spikes, do we pay extra for bursts?
[05:12] Liam: We have burst capacity options. Dedicated commit gives baseline capacity; you can enable burst-to-hosted fallbacks where overflow uses hosted nodes at a surcharge, or buy burst credits. That gives predictability while avoiding dropped requests.
[05:23] Sara: Let's talk sample math for our 400 rps realtime peak: assume avg prompt 250 tokens (200 cached), response 100 tokens. Effective tokens per request ~150. At 400 rps that's 60k tokens/sec, about 172M tokens/hour, 4.1B tokens/day if constant. That scales fast.
[05:44] Liam: Right. Multiply by days and months - at full sustained peak you'd hit enormous numbers. But real traffic has diurnal patterns. The pricing spreadsheet will model peaks vs avg. Also we recommend prefix caching to reduce the effective prompt token counts in the realtime path.
[05:58] Evelyn: For batch 2M nightly with long contexts 2k tokens, we expect heavy GPU time—would you run that on dedicated batch nodes to maximize throughput?
[06:07] Liam: Yes. For batch, you optimize for throughput—larger batch sizes, quantized models, and longer sequences are GPU-friendly. Many customers run batch on dedicated cheaper nodes or schedule overnight to smooth costs.
[06:18] Jonas: Any hidden costs - e.g., kernel licensing, storage, egress?
[06:22] Mia: Good callout. Hosted pricing includes compute and inference service; additional line items can be long-term storage for audit logs or high-retention observability, or extra support / enterprise features. For private deployments, egress and infra costs are on you. We'll enumerate those in the doc.
[06:37] Sara: Do you have examples of customers similar size who moved from hosted to dedicated and their cost delta?
[06:44] Liam: Yes—an anonymized case: a trading analytics firm with similar realtime/batch split moved to dedicated and saw 30-50% reduction in per-token compute costs at 70% utilization, plus predictability on monthly spend. We'll share that case study.
[06:58] Evelyn: For evaluation, we want to run a benchmark—can you run with our workload sample and show per-token breakdown with and without prefix cache and with quantized models?
[07:07] Liam: Absolutely. Typical benchmark includes three axes: latency p95, tokens/sec throughput, and cost per 1M tokens. We'll run hosted and dedicated (if you provide expected sustained windows) and show savings from caching and batching.
[07:18] Jonas: Timeline: we want numbers this week for finance and a technical deep dive next week. Is that feasible?
[07:23] Mia: Yes. We'll send the pricing spreadsheet and a benchmark template today, aim to complete an initial run and get back with results in 5 business days.
[07:30] Sara: One more - SSO and KMS. For private/dedicated do you support customer-managed KMS and SAML?
[07:36] Mia: Yes, dedicated and private have integrations for KMS/HSM and SAML/SSO and we provide audit logs. Hosted also supports customer-managed keys for some plans. We'll attach the security docs.
[07:46] Evelyn: Great. I also want to understand how billing handles cached tokens - like are cached tokens billed once or per request?
[07:53] Liam: Billed per request only for non-cached tokens. If a prefix is served from KV cache, we don't charge for recomputing that prefix tokens; however some models may have internal accounting differences—our billing tries to reflect effective compute saved. We'll include an explainer in the spreadsheet.
[08:07] Jonas: Any SLA guarantees on latency for dedicated?
[08:11] Mia: We have SLA-backed uptime and latency targets on enterprise dedicated plans. We'll share specifics; they vary by commit tier.
[08:19] Evelyn: Ok, recap then next steps?
[08:22] Mia: Recap: we'll send pricing spreadsheet with hosted vs dedicated vs private modeling, include examples with caching and quantization assumptions; Liam will prepare benchmark checklist and run options; Evelyn to share workload sample; schedule technical deep dive next week.
[08:37] Jonas: Sounds good.
[08:39] Sara: Thanks, everyone.
[08:41] Mia: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs.
